name: Palau
summary: About 340 islands in western Micronesia, ruled by Spain, Germany, Japan and then the US (UN Trust Territory); independent in free association with the US since 1994.

knownFor.label: Stone money
knownFor.note: Huge Rai stones quarried here for Yap.

location.value: Western Pacific east of the Philippines; about 460 km².

terrain.value: About 340 islands: volcanic Babeldaob, the largest; the limestone Rock Islands; and low coral atolls such as Kayangel, inside a large reef lagoon.

climate.value: Hot, humid tropical climate with heavy rain all year; it lies mostly south of the main typhoon belt, though typhoons such as Haiyan (2013) can strike.

resources.value: Coral reefs and rich marine life that draw divers, tuna fisheries, and limited farmland on Babeldaob.

disasters.value: Cyclones, droughts and rising sea levels.

population.value: About 18,000 people (2024 estimate), mostly Palauans, with many Filipino and other foreign workers.

urbanisation.value: Most people live in and around Koror, the old capital and main town; the capital moved to Ngerulmud on Babeldaob in 2006.

disease.value: Diabetes and heart disease from imported food.

migration.value: Palauans can live and work in the United States under the Compact of Free Association, and many have moved to Guam, Hawaii and the US mainland.

economicBase.value: Tourism, especially diving and visitors from East Asia, along with US Compact funding, fishing and government jobs.

tradeRoutes.value: Imports arrive by sea at Malakal port near Koror; flights from Roman Tmetuchl International Airport connect Palau with Guam, Taiwan and other Asian destinations.

wealth.value: A middle- to high-income economy by Pacific standards, with income per person among the highest in Micronesia, largely from tourism and US funding.

moneyAndTax.value: The US dollar is the official currency; the government relies on taxes, fees charged to visitors and grants under the Compact.

inequality.value: Gap between the capital and outer islands.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic modelled on the US, with an elected president, a two-chamber congress (Olbiil Era Kelulau) and a council of traditional chiefs.

keyRulers.value: Haruo Remeliik, first president (1981–85, assassinated), and Lazarus Salii (1985–88); the Compact of Free Association with the United States took effect in 1994.

succession.value: The president and vice-president are elected directly every four years, and a president may serve no more than two terms in a row.

institutions.value: Olbiil Era Kelulau (congress); Council of Chiefs.

stability.value: Peaceful elections and handovers since 1994, after a troubled 1980s that saw the assassination of the first president, Haruo Remeliik (1985).

eliteConflict.value: Politics turns on rivalries between clans, states and leading families rather than formal parties, which Palau does not have.

armyAndTech.value: Palau has no military; under the Compact of Free Association the United States is responsible for its defence, and a small marine police patrols its waters.

majorWars.value: No wars since independence; in 1944 US and Japanese forces fought the bloody Battle of Peleliu, and US troops also took Angaur.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1994; Palau voted not to join the Federated States of Micronesia in 1978 and adopted its own constitution in 1981.

alliancesRivals.value: Compact of Free Association with the United States (since 1986), which gives US defence and aid. Recognises Taiwan.

inventions.value: Traditional navigation by stars and swells.

scienceEducation.value: University of the South Pacific campuses.

openness.value: Open to visitors and trade but dependent on imports; its National Marine Sanctuary law (2015) closed most of its waters to commercial fishing.

communicationTransport.value: A causeway and the Japan–Palau Friendship Bridge (2002) link Koror to Babeldaob, which has a ring road; boats serve the outer islands.

religion.value: Mostly Christian, about half Roman Catholic with many Protestants; Modekngei, a local faith mixing Christian and Palauan beliefs, also has followers.

languageWriting.value: Palauan and English are official; Sonsorolese and Tobian are spoken on the southwest islands, and some older people speak Japanese.

artsArchitecture.value: The bai, a tall-gabled men’s meeting house painted with legends, and carved storyboards, which became a popular craft during Japanese rule.

socialStructure.value: Matrilineal clans in which land and titles pass through women; senior women choose, and can remove, the male chiefs.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Palauan identity based on clans, language and custom, combined with close ties to the United States.

dailyLife.value: Fish, taro and tapioca alongside imported rice and canned food; many people work for the government or in tourism.

neighbours.value: The Philippines and Indonesia to the west and south, the Federated States of Micronesia to the east, and the US territory of Guam to the northeast.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity from Spanish Catholic missions and later Protestant churches, together with Modekngei and respect for customary chiefs.

colonisation.value: Spanish, German (1899), Japanese (1914), then US trust territory (1947–94).

riseSignals.value: Became independent in free association with the United States on 1 October 1994, ending the last part of the UN Trust Territory.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; tourism grew strongly in the 2000s and 2010s before the 2020 pandemic halted visitors.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still an independent republic in free association with the United States; it joined the United Nations in December 1994.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
